explanation: Mixture with no clear common thread: verb endings in legal case headers (Dec[ided], Arg[ued]), license boilerplate words ('distributing', 'name'), code punctuation and identifiers (' =', ')', '}', 'h' in class names), path components (Users, USER), and assorted prose tokens. Hard to predict; legal-opinion header words and license text fire most reliably.

Fires on tokens inside geopolitical, ethnic or regional descriptions: nationality/ethnic adjectives and place-name fragments (Arab, Sl-avic, Urom-i, Pakistan, World, National) and the connecting words in phrases about regions, states, and political bodies ('between', 'from', 'of' in 'Region of Niger'). Strongest on world-affairs or geography text about countries, peoples, and coalitions; weak elsewhere.

Fires on technical tokens in networking/software-infrastructure and climate-emissions contexts: version numbers in 'Apache License, Version 2.[0]', 'governed' in 'Use of this source code is governed', protocol/system names (AWS4, tcphdr, SELinux, SDN, web servers), and 'carbon'/'emission'/'abatement' in climate text. Two clusters: software/network boilerplate and carbon-emissions vocabulary.
Fires essentially only on a '0' digit token inside long runs of zeros (e.g. '0000000[0]0005'); nearly everything else is ~0%.

Fires on characters inside random alphanumeric strings, especially short-link/URL IDs (pic.twitter.com/, t.co/, jsfiddle, youtube ids) and tokens/keys/hashes, strongest on a digit near the start of the random ID. Weaker on initials in names and digits in math expressions.

Fires on content words (often the head noun/verb) in scientific, medical or social-issue abstract-style prose about problems, risks and their trends (corruption, dependence, gambling, pregnancies, recurrence, increase, spread, accident). Strongest in medical/public-health abstracts; weaker in casual prose.

Fires mainly on the opening parenthesis ' (' that precedes an acronym after a spelled-out technical name (e.g. 'ATP-binding cassette (ABC)', 'Total knee arthroplasty (TKA)'); also on similar title/ticker separators (':' in 'Nasdaq: NTGN', 'Oblivion') and the first digit of yardage in football passes. Main job is the acronym-introducing parenthesis.

Mixture: tokens in Russian and CJK text (word-internal pieces), plus English prepositions/function words in technical or math instructions ('with', 'to' in 'convert X to Y', 'be' in 'Let y be', 'by', 'if'). No single unifying feature beyond non-English/technical-instruction context.

Mixture: 'of' in 'Use of this source code' and 'use of this website' boilerplate, 'using' in cookie notices, plus a variety of technical/scientific word fragments (Lagrangian, infty, Abelian, stereo-, hypocycloidal) and code/assembly tokens. Boilerplate 'use of' is the clearest piece, rest is scattered.
Mixture: 'over' in 'all over (the world/place)', '.io' in 'import java.io', escape-code digits, Romanian/Vietnamese/CJK word pieces, markdown table dashes and code fences. Several unrelated triggers.

Fires on a technical/specialized noun (or noun-piece) that names a property, quantity or concept in expository text, often the head of a noun phrase after 'the' or as the key term (age, time, tilt, draft, ranking, pharmacokinetic, extraversion, division, bioavailability, Buffer). Roughly a 'key domain term' detector; prediction is fuzzy.

Fires on internal subword pieces of proper names, especially transliterated foreign place and person names (Kilkenny, Shandong, Zemplín, Zelenskiy, Bokova, Xiantao) and some Spanish/Hungarian word pieces; also odd items like 'host' in Docker plugin lists. Mainly mid-word fragments of proper nouns.

Fires strongest on a '0' within long runs of zeros, and moderately on 'import' in Python 'from X.Y import Z' lines and on template opening tags ('<?php', '<%='), plus some CJK characters. Two-to-several code/formatting triggers.

Mixture: second byte of split multibyte characters (CJK, emoji, Greek), JS 'promisify', comment divider lines, and assorted English word-ending pieces (-ists, retrospect, adversity, fullest). No coherent concept.
